lines.text: A three-digit number can change what you pay for a car, an apartment, and even a phone plan.
It's your credit score. Today we're going to take it apart, piece by piece, so you know exactly how it works.
Chapter one. What a credit score actually is.
A credit score is a number that sums up how reliably you've paid back money you borrowed.
The most widely used one, the FICO score, runs from 300 to 850.
lines.say: The most widely used one, the FICO score, runs from three hundred to eight hundred fifty.

lines.text: It's calculated from your credit reports, which are kept by three big credit bureaus.

scene.def: A credit bureau is a company that keeps your [credit report].
scene.example: The big three: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion

lines.text: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

scene.def: A credit bureau is a company that keeps your [credit report].
scene.example: The big three: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion

lines.text: Your credit report is the record. Your score is a grade calculated from that record.
And you don't have just one score. There are different models, like FICO and VantageScore, and lenders pick which one they use.

scene.headline: You have [more than one] score
scene.sub: FICO, VantageScore and versions of each

lines.text: Why it matters: a higher score can mean lower interest rates, smaller deposits, and more yeses when you apply.

scene.title: What a higher score can get you

lines.text: Chapter two. The five things that make up your score.
FICO publishes how much each part counts. Here's the whole recipe.

scene.title: What makes up a FICO score

lines.text: Payment history is the biggest piece, at thirty-five percent. Amounts owed is next, at thirty.

scene.title: What makes up a FICO score

lines.text: Together, those two are almost two-thirds of your score. So let's start there.

scene.label: Payment history + amounts owed
scene.note: Two habits do [most of the work].

lines.say: Together, those two are almost two thirds of your score. So let's start there.

lines.text: Chapter three. Payment history.
This one is simple: do you pay your bills on time?
A payment usually gets reported as late once it's thirty days past due.

scene.label: When a payment is usually reported late

lines.say: A payment usually gets reported as late once it's thirty days past due.

lines.text: And a late payment can stay on your credit report for up to seven years.

scene.label: How long a late payment can stay
scene.note: It fades over time, but it [lingers].

lines.say: And a late payment can stay on your credit report for up to seven years.

lines.text: Paying a day or two late usually means a late fee, not a hit to your credit report. The thirty-day mark is what counts.

scene.headline: 1 day late: a fee. [30 days]: your report.

lines.text: If you do miss one, pay it as fast as you can. The longer it goes, the worse it gets, at sixty and ninety days.

scene.title: Late payments get worse with time

lines.text: The easiest fix is autopay for at least the minimum, so a busy week never becomes a late payment.
Chapter four. Amounts owed.
A big part of this is your credit utilization.

scene.def: Utilization: how much of your credit limit you're [using].

lines.text: If your limit is five thousand dollars and you owe one thousand, you're using twenty percent.

scene.def: Utilization: how much of your credit limit you're [using].

lines.text: Lower usage generally helps your score. Here's how the same five thousand dollar limit looks at different balances.
A common rule of thumb is to stay under thirty percent, and lower is better.
Paying your balance before the statement date can also lower the number that gets reported.
The good news: card balances are usually reported monthly, so paying them down can show up in your score fairly quickly.
Chapter five. The last three pieces.
Length of history is fifteen percent. Older accounts help, so closing your oldest card can shorten your history.
New credit covers hard inquiries.

scene.def: A hard inquiry: a lender checks your credit because you [applied].
scene.example: On your report 2 years, counted for about 1

lines.text: A hard inquiry stays on your report for two years, and FICO scores only count it for about one year.

scene.def: A hard inquiry: a lender checks your credit because you [applied].
scene.example: On your report 2 years, counted for about 1

lines.text: Shopping around for a mortgage or car loan? Scoring models usually count several of those checks in a short window as one.

scene.headline: Rate shopping counts [as one]
scene.sub: Within a short window, often 14 to 45 days

lines.text: Opening several new cards at once is different. It adds inquiries and lowers the average age of your accounts.

scene.headline: Many new cards at once [costs you]

lines.text: And credit mix means having different kinds, like a card and an installment loan. It's the smallest piece, so never borrow just to improve it.

scene.headline: Never borrow just to [raise a score]

lines.text: Chapter six. Checking your credit, for free.
You can get free credit reports from all three bureaus every week at AnnualCreditReport dot com.
Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry, so it doesn't hurt your score.

scene.headline: Checking your own credit [doesn't hurt it]

lines.text: Look for accounts you don't recognize or payments marked late by mistake, and dispute errors with the bureau.

items.d: Wrong late marks can be disputed

lines.text: Chapter seven. Starting from zero.
If you have no credit history, you can't have a score yet. Here are the common ways people start.

scene.title: Common ways to start building credit

items.d: You put down a deposit as the limit

lines.text: Whichever you use, the same rules apply: small balances, paid on time, every month.
Chapter eight. Myths that cost people money.
Myth: you need to carry a balance and pay interest to build credit.

scene.myth: You have to carry a balance to build credit.
scene.fact: Paying in full still builds credit, with [zero interest].

lines.text: Fact: paying your full balance still shows on-time payments and low usage. You never have to pay interest to build credit.

scene.myth: You have to carry a balance to build credit.
scene.fact: Paying in full still builds credit, with [zero interest].

lines.text: Myth: a higher income means a higher score. Fact: income isn't part of your credit score at all.

scene.myth: A bigger paycheck raises your score.
scene.fact: Income is [not part] of your credit score.

lines.text: Myth: closing an unused card always helps. It can actually hurt, because your total limit shrinks and your usage goes up.

scene.myth: Closing unused cards helps your score.
scene.fact: It can raise your usage and [hurt it].

lines.text: Chapter nine. How long the bad stuff lasts.
Late payments and collections can stay for up to seven years. Some bankruptcies stay for up to ten.

scene.title: How long negative marks can stay

lines.text: But their impact fades. Recent on-time payments matter more than old mistakes.
So here's the whole thing in five moves.
Pay on time. Keep balances low. Keep old accounts open. And apply only when you need to.
And check your reports every few months, for free, so nothing surprises you.
Do those consistently, and your score takes care of itself over time.
That's the money. See you at the next bell.
